design_detail: Inpatient, within-participant, double-blind, placebo-controlled human laboratory study over 2 weeks (four sessions). Single intranasal doses of methamphetamine HCl 0 (lactose placebo), 12, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg, each given once to each of 11 non-treatment-seeking people who regularly used methamphetamine intranasally. Plasma methamphetamine, heart rate and blood pressure, 44 visual-analogue ratings, a drug-effect questionnaire, a price question and five computerized cognitive/psychomotor tasks were measured before and repeatedly after each dose (to 4 h; plasma to 24 h). Dose order: ascending for the first 2 participants (for safety), counterbalanced thereafter; the paper does not describe the order as randomized.
can_establish: That in 11 experienced, medically screened people who use methamphetamine intranasally, single laboratory doses of 12 to 50 mg/70 kg raised heart rate, blood pressure and ratings such as 'high' and 'good drug effect' relative to placebo, with these effects peaking within about 15 minutes while venous plasma concentrations kept rising for about 4 hours.
cannot_establish: Effects in people without methamphetamine experience, in women (2 of 11), with repeated or binge-pattern doses, above 50 mg/70 kg or by other routes; whether the plasma-effect dissociation has consequences for toxicity after repeated doses (not tested); or the absolute size of the cardiovascular, plasma and performance changes (shown only in figures).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement and word of mouth: newspaper advertisements and word-of-mouth referrals in New York City; volunteers not seeking treatment for their methamphetamine use (Methods › Participants). Payment is not mentioned.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Current DSM-IV methamphetamine abuse (n=2) or dependence (n=9); not seeking treatment; passed medical and psychiatric evaluations; within normal weight range by the 1983 Metropolitan Life tables. The paper states no participant met criteria for any other Axis I disorder. Further exclusion criteria (for example cardiovascular disease) are not listed (Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Mean age 30.7 years (SD 6.4); 9 men (3 Black, 3 Latino, 3 White) and 2 women (1 Black, 1 White); education 12 to 17 years (mean 13.7); BMI 24.1 (SD 4.4) (Methods › Participants).
sample.attrition: One additional man began but did not complete the protocol because he did not comply with study procedures; he is not in the analysis. Table 1 peak means for two items ('nose burning', methamphetamine craving) fit 10 rather than 11 participants (editors' arithmetic check, see reporting issues); no missing data are reported.
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited, regular, mostly dependent intranasal users in New York City, screened for medical and psychiatric health, not seeking treatment, 9 of 11 men. Every participant had already received the highest study dose in an open pre-study session (Methods › Pre-Study Training). Findings may not generalize to less experienced people, to women, to people with medical or psychiatric comorbidity, or to people who smoke or inject methamphetamine.

exposure.measurement: Experimental administration of methamphetamine HCl supplied by NIDA and prepared by the institute pharmacy, or lactose placebo, double-blind; plasma methamphetamine measured from an intravenous line. Participants' usual use was self-reported. Urine was tested before each session for amphetamines, cocaine, morphine derivatives and THC, but the results are not reported (Methods › Drugs; Experimental Day).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single intranasal doses of 0, 12, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg (weight-adjusted, single dose capped at 60 mg), one per session, sessions at least 72 h apart (two per week). Participants' own reported use: 3.6 (SD 1.7) days per week, US$100 (SD 75) per week on the drug, 6.1 (SD 5.4) years of use, all primarily intranasal. The paper quotes a local street price of $100 to $300 per gram, which implies roughly 0.3 to 1 g of street product of unknown purity per week (editors' calculation). Comparison with use outside the laboratory: the authors note, citing anecdotal reports, that use often involves repeated doses every 0.5 to 3 h over several days; only single doses were tested (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Current use: cocaine 6 of 11 (1 to 4 times a week), alcohol 7 of 11 (1.5 to 15 drinks a week), cannabis 7 of 11 (1 to 6 times a week), tobacco 8 of 11 (2 to 20 cigarettes a day); other drug use infrequent (Methods › Participants). Handled by inpatient residence from several days before the first session to study end (no unescorted leave, no visitors) and pre-session urine tests (results not reported). Whether nicotine dependence was assessed is not stated.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Inpatient from several days before the first session (exact washout not stated); at least 72 h between study doses; smokers refrained from 1 h before and during each session. Abstinence from non-study drugs is supported by residence; urine results are not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-participant placebo condition (lactose); each participant served as their own control.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-participant). Dose order counterbalanced within and between participants after the first two, who received ascending order for safety; the sequences used are not reported (Methods › Design).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant to the within-person drug-placebo contrasts. The relevant unmeasured factors are tolerance (all regular users), expectancy (all had received the 50 mg/70 kg dose openly before testing) and period or carryover effects (not analysed).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants as the active conditions; see polysubstance.

outcomes.instruments: Venous plasma methamphetamine at baseline, 5, 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min and at 6, 12 and 24 h; heart rate and systolic and diastolic pressure by automated monitor at baseline and 5 to 240 min, with continuous ECG; computerized 100-mm visual-analogue scales (41 effect items plus 3 craving items: want methamphetamine, alcohol, a cigarette) at the same times except 30 min; Drug-Effect Questionnaire at 90 min (good effects, bad effects, strength, take again on 0 to 4; liking on -4 to +4); price willing to pay for the dose ($0 to $20) at session end; computerized battery at 15, 60, 120, 180 and 240 min: Digit-Symbol Substitution Task (DSST), repeated acquisition, divided attention task, rapid information task, immediate and delayed digit recall (Methods › Experimental Day; Subjective-Effects and Cognitive/Psychomotor Battery).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard human-laboratory measures for abuse liability and performance; norms are not needed for within-person contrasts. Participants were trained on the tasks in two 3 to 4 h sessions to limit learning effects (Methods › Pre-Study Training).
outcomes.operationalization: Effects defined as dose differences in two-factor (dose x time) repeated-measures ANOVA with planned comparisons, and as peak (or lowest) values per dose in Table 1. Performance improvement meant shorter hit latency and higher maximum tracking speed (divided attention task) and more attempts and correct responses (DSST). Adverse events were not defined or operationalized.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across outcomes: each measure tested at P<0.05, with Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity where appropriate. 59 is a lower bound (44 VAS items, 5 questionnaire items, price, 3 cardiovascular measures, plasma level, and 5 tasks counted once although each yields several scores). Table 1 lists only items with significant effects.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Drug administration double-blind; blinding integrity (participants' or staff guesses) not assessed. Outcomes are self-rated or automated.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper gives F statistics and P values, peak means (SEM) in Table 1, and time courses in figures only; no effect sizes or confidence intervals. Dose main effects: plasma F(3,330)=121.57; heart rate F(3,240)=13.05; systolic F(3,240)=43.37; diastolic F(3,240)=33.52; good drug effect F(3,180)=14.93; stimulated F(3,180)=11.03; hungry F(3,180)=11.65; tired F(3,180)=10.77; take again F(3,30)=14.01; price F(3,30)=10.39. Editors' calculation from Table 1 peak means, with SD = SEM x square root of 11 and the difference divided by the average of the two condition SDs (ignores the within-person correlation, so approximate): good drug effect vs placebo d about 1.6 (12 mg), 3.4 (25 mg), 5.6 (50 mg); 'high' 1.6, 3.0, 3.7; 'stimulated' 1.1, 1.8, 2.9; questionnaire liking 1.1, 1.7, 2.0; hunger -1.6, -2.3, -2.7. Plasma, cardiovascular and performance magnitudes cannot be extracted (figures are images).
analysis.covariates: None; within-participant comparisons. Session order (period) was not included in the model.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 shows only VAS and questionnaire items with significant effects; items such as anxious, paranoid, bad drug effect, confused, nauseous, headache and want alcohol or a cigarette are not reported. Three of five tasks (repeated acquisition, rapid information, digit recall) are summarized only as showing no significant effect. The comparisons reported (each active dose vs placebo; 50 vs 12 and 25 mg) differ from the planned contrasts described in Data Analysis, and the peak-value analysis behind Table 1 is not described in Methods.
analysis.power: Not reported; n=11. Adequate for the large subjective and cardiovascular effects; non-significant results (no performance disruption, no effects on three tasks) cannot exclude small or moderate effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 11 experienced intranasal users, single doses of 12 to 50 mg/70 kg produced large dose-related increases in ratings such as 'good drug effect', 'high' and 'stimulated', lowered hunger and tiredness, and raised heart rate and blood pressure (sizes shown only in figures); subjective and cardiovascular effects peaked within about 15 min while venous plasma concentrations rose for about 4 h. Performance improved on the divided attention task at all active doses and on the DSST at 12 and 25 mg only; no other task changed significantly. Ratings of jittery, sweating, heart beating faster and nose burning were higher than placebo at 50 mg (some also at lower doses).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion describe the effects as orderly and primarily positive, the conclusion adds that the drug produced them without noticeable adverse consequences, and both say the plasma-effect dissociation might matter for toxicity after repeated doses (Abstract; Discussion, last paragraph). The discussion states the 12 and 25 mg doses improved performance more than 50 mg and that no dose produced significant performance disruption (Discussion, 1st paragraph). Gaps: (1) the phrase 'without producing noticeable adverse consequences' sits beside measured rises in blood pressure and heart rate and in ratings of jittery, sweating, palpitations and nose burning, adverse events were not defined, and the sample was small, screened and experienced; (2) the advantage of 12 and 25 mg over 50 mg on the DSST rests on significance at two doses but not the third, with no direct comparison reported; (3) no performance disruption is a non-significant result in 11 people; (4) the toxicity and route remarks concern repeated dosing and other routes, which were not studied; (5) the abstract's split into less and more complicated tasks is not defined in Methods; (6) the discussion's statement that mood was consistently enhanced (citing 'content') contrasts with Table 1, where 'content' rose only at 50 mg.

timeline.event: Harris et al. (2003): single 50 mg intranasal dose given together with deuterated intravenous methamphetamine, no placebo; bioavailability 79% intranasal; increases in positive ratings, blood pressure and heart rate (as summarized in this paper's Introduction).
This study: first placebo-controlled intranasal dose-response study (0 to 50 mg/70 kg) in 11 regular users.

replication.where_it_stands: A small, single-laboratory study. The same laboratory later tested intranasal methamphetamine against d-amphetamine in a self-administration design (Kirkpatrick et al., 2012; appraised on its own card), which is the closest conceptual replication of the acute subjective and cardiovascular profile. Repeated-dose and larger-sample data on the plasma-effect dissociation were not found in this reading.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA19559 (Acknowledgments). Study methamphetamine supplied by NIDA (Methods › Drugs).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that, apart from income from their primary employer, they received no financial support or compensation from any individual or corporate entity in the past 3 years for research or professional service, and hold no personal financial holdings that could be perceived as a conflict (Disclosure/Conflicts of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University (Department of Psychiatry; Department of Psychology). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A placebo-controlled study with randomized dose sequences that gives repeated intranasal doses at intervals seen in real-world use, with dense early arterial and venous sampling, blinding checks, prespecified adverse-event definitions and a larger, sex-balanced sample, would show whether cardiovascular and subjective effects track or dissociate from accumulating plasma concentrations.

domains.note: Order counterbalanced, not described as randomized; the first 2 participants received ascending order; allocation concealment not described. Within-person contrasts remove between-person confounding.
At least 72 h between doses, but period was not modelled, the 2 ascending-order participants confound dose with session, and carryover was not tested (24-h plasma values appear only in Figure 1).
Double-blind, but all participants had received the 50 mg/70 kg dose openly in a pre-study session and were experienced users; blinding integrity not assessed. No deviations reported.
11 of 12 completed; one non-completer excluded. Two VAS items appear to lack one participant's data (editors' arithmetic check).
Self-ratings by possibly unblinded experienced users (some concerns); cardiovascular and plasma measures automated or assayed (low).
Only significant VAS items tabulated; three tasks reported only as non-significant; reported comparisons differ from the planned contrasts; peak analysis not described; no protocol.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 is applied as for a crossover trial, adapted because the order was counterbalanced rather than randomized. The large effects on subjective ratings, cardiovascular measures and plasma concentrations are unlikely to be explained by these concerns. Non-random order, possible functional unblinding after open exposure to the top dose, an error term that inflates degrees of freedom, and selective tabulation lower confidence in the smaller effects (performance, single VAS items) and in the claim that there were no adverse consequences.

key_findings.finding: Participants: 11 completers (9 men, 2 women; mean age 30.7, SD 6.4) with current DSM-IV methamphetamine abuse (2) or dependence (9), all primarily intranasal users, using on 3.6 (SD 1.7) days a week for 6.1 (SD 5.4) years, not seeking treatment.

Each participant received the highest dose (50 mg/70 kg) on a separate day before the study for familiarization and safety monitoring; no untoward events were noted. Study doses were then given once each, at least 72 h apart, ascending for the first 2 participants and counterbalanced thereafter.

Plasma methamphetamine rose dose-dependently (F(3,330)=121.57, P<0.0001); every active dose differed from placebo and from each other (P<0.005); concentrations peaked 4 h after dosing and declined over the following hours. Concentration values appear only in Figure 1 (image).
key_findings.locator: Results › Plasma Methamphetamine Levels; Figure 1, upper left
key_findings.note: No samples were taken between 240 min and 6 h, so the time of peak is bounded by the sampling schedule.

key_findings.finding: Heart rate (F(3,240)=13.05), systolic pressure (F(3,240)=43.37) and diastolic pressure (F(3,240)=33.52) increased (all P<0.0001); all active doses differed from placebo (P<0.04); for heart rate 25 and 50 mg exceeded 12 mg (P<0.05); for systolic and diastolic pressure 50 mg exceeded both lower doses (P<0.0001); peak cardiovascular effects within 15 min. Magnitudes in bpm and mmHg appear only in Figure 1.
key_findings.note: Denominator df imply a pooled within-session error term; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: 'Good drug effect' (F(3,180)=14.93) and 'stimulated' (F(3,180)=11.03) increased (P<0.001), with all active doses above placebo and 50 mg above 12 and 25 mg (P<0.03); 'hungry' (F(3,180)=11.65) and 'tired' (F(3,180)=10.77) decreased at all active doses (P<0.006); peak subjective effects 15 min after dosing.

Ratings with an adverse character, placebo vs 50 mg peak means: jittery 7.36 vs 24.82, sweating 2.09 vs 25.09, heart beating faster 11.27 vs 43.18, nose burning 2.60 vs 28.00 (all significant vs placebo); heart beating faster and nose burning were also raised at 25 mg, jittery at 12 mg. 'Irritable' fell at 50 mg (37.55 to 18.27).
Methamphetamine craving was high under placebo (peak 79.00 of 100) and was lower than placebo only at 25 mg (70.00; F=4.44), not at 12 mg (71.80) or 50 mg (71.30).
key_findings.note: These means fit 10 rather than 11 participants (editors' arithmetic check).

key_findings.finding: Desire to take the drug again (F(3,30)=14.01) and the price participants would pay for the dose (F(3,30)=10.39) rose with dose (P<0.001); values appear only in Figure 3.

Divided attention task: all active doses shortened mean hit latency and raised maximum tracking speed (P<0.05). DSST: 12 and 25 mg, but not 50 mg, increased attempts and correct responses (P<0.03). No other significant performance effects (repeated acquisition, rapid information, digit recall). Values appear only in Figure 4.

reporting_issues.issue: Dose main effects carry denominator degrees of freedom of 330 (plasma), 240 (cardiovascular) and 180 (subjective ratings). A repeated-measures test of dose in 11 participants has (4-1) x (11-1) = 30 error df; the printed values equal 30 x (number of time points - 1), so the dose x time residual appears to have been used as the error term.
reporting_issues.consequence: Tests of dose are anti-conservative because repeated time points within a session are treated as independent information about dose. Large effects (plasma, blood pressure, good drug effect) would remain significant; marginal effects on single items are less certain. Questionnaire and price items, measured once per session, carry the expected df of 30.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods say subjective ratings were taken at the cardiovascular time points with two exceptions but name only one (no 30-min ratings); the df of 180 imply 7 rather than 8 time points.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the second omitted time point is not identified.

reporting_issues.issue: The planned contrasts described in Data Analysis (placebo vs all active doses; 12 mg vs the two larger doses; 25 vs 50 mg) differ from the comparisons reported (each active dose vs placebo; 50 mg vs 12 and vs 25 mg), and the peak-value analysis in Table 1 is not described in Methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reported comparisons were not the pre-specified ones; with at least 59 measures and no correction, some single-item differences may be chance findings.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints F=5.51 for 'forgetful' at 50 mg without the mark for a difference from placebo, while items with similar F values (irritable 5.45, jittery 5.65) carry it; only the mark for a difference from 12 mg is shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a mark is missing or the F refers to another contrast; whether 50 mg raised forgetfulness relative to placebo is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Peak means for 'nose burning' and methamphetamine craving are exact multiples of 1/10 and not of 1/11 (e.g. 23.70, 71.80), unlike every other item, consistent with ratings from 10 of the 11 participants; no missing data are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' arithmetic check, valid if ratings were recorded as whole millimetres; if correct, one participant's data are missing for these items without explanation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says methamphetamine consistently enhanced mood, citing ratings of 'content', but Table 1 shows 'content' raised only at 50 mg (F=0.07 at 12 mg and 0.13 at 25 mg).
reporting_issues.consequence: Text overstates the consistency of the mood effect.

reporting_issues.issue: Urine toxicology was collected before every session but no results are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Exposure to non-study drugs during the inpatient stay cannot be checked from the paper.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4918768 (author manuscript; all sections, Table 1 rendered as text, author information, acknowledgments and disclosure read; Figures 1 to 4 are images and their values were not extracted; no supplementary files)
